title: Evaluating large language models for accuracy incentivizes hallucinations
authors: Adam Tauman Kalai, Ofir Nachum, Santosh S. Vempala, Edwin Zhang
note: This work analyzes how training and evaluation reward guessing, and argues for scoring systems that make acknowledging uncertainty a better strategy.
problem: Why do models guess instead of admitting uncertainty?
limitation: Changing the scoring rule is not a guarantee that hallucinations disappear.

title: Models That Prove Their Own Correctness

note: Introduces a trainable safety layer that constrains a robot’s actions to satisfy specified requirements, with guarantees that depend on the model of the robot and its environment.

title: Consensus Sampling for Safer Generative AI
authors: A. Kalai, Y. Tauman Kalai, O. Zamir
note: Selects an output from several models, or declines to answer, with a provable limit on the risk of harmful output relative to the more reliable models. The method requires access to each model’s output probabilities. Producing useful answers also depends on sufficient overlap among the reliable models’ output distributions.

title: Governing AI Agents
note: Examines the responsibilities and limits of authority that arise when AI agents act for people, and explains why existing approaches to monitoring and accountability may be insufficient.

title: On the Impossibility of Separating Intelligence from Judgment: The Computational Intractability of Filtering for AI Alignment
authors: S. Ball, G. Gluch, S. Goldwasser, F. Kreuter, O. Reingold, G. Rothblum
note: Establishes computational barriers to external prompt and output filtering under cryptographic hardness assumptions and specified relationships between the model and filter. These worst-case results do not say that filtering has no practical value.

highlight.title: Understanding the limits of filtering
highlight.summary: Cryptographic constructions expose computational limits of certain input and output filters. The results depend on explicit hardness assumptions and formal settings.

title: Planting Undetectable Backdoors in Machine Learning Models
authors: S. Goldwasser, M. Kim, V. Vaikuntanathan, O. Zamir
note: Shows how a model can appear to function normally while containing a hidden trigger that changes its behavior. Under cryptographic assumptions, such backdoors can evade inspection within feasible computing limits.

title: A Cryptographic Perspective on Mitigation vs. Detection in Machine Learning
note: Shows that, for certain tasks involving generated outputs, a defense can limit harmful behavior even when the harmful inputs cannot be efficiently identified.

title: Pseudorandom Error-Correcting Codes
note: Introduces a way to hide information in apparently random data while allowing a key holder to recover it after specified alterations. This underpins methods for watermarking AI-generated content and hiding communication.

title: Undetectable Conversations Between AI Agents via Pseudorandom Noise-Resilient Key Exchange
note: Shows how cooperating AI agents could hide secret exchanges within ordinary-looking messages, even without a shared secret at the outset.

title: How to sketch a learning algorithm
note: How would a model behave if some training data had been left out? A sketch of the learning algorithm predicts these counterfactual outputs, supporting data deletion queries and attribution, with error and failure guarantees under a stability assumption. The method predicts counterfactual measurements rather than outputting a retrained model. Evidence for the stability assumption comes from small-scale microgpt experiments.
